column3: At about 600 meters, the slim, twisting tower on the Pearl River is nicknamed the Small Waist. It glows with colored lights at night and has a high-up observation deck.
A tiny island of tree-lined streets and 19th-century European-style buildings, once the foreign concession in Guangzhou and now a peaceful place to walk.
A grand clan hall built in the 1890s, covered with carved stone, wood, ceramic figures and colored plaster, a showcase of Cantonese craft.
A big hill park in the middle of Guangzhou. Its Five Rams statue recalls the legend that five immortals on rams brought grain to the city.
An old shopping street of arcaded buildings, packed with snack shops and old brands, a lively place for an evening stroll.
A boat ride along the Pearl River in the evening, passing glowing skyscrapers, old bridges and the Canton Tower in lights.
A green mountain right beside the city, with winding paths, springs and viewpoints, where residents go to hike at the weekend.
Guangzhou's morning tea is a long, relaxed meal of dim sum, with small steamers, pots of tea and family talk. Some say it is the heart of Cantonese food culture.
A classic dim sum dumpling in a thin, translucent wrapper, with whole juicy shrimp inside. Making a good one takes real skill.
Smooth, silky sheets of steamed rice batter rolled around shrimp, beef or pork, then served with a splash of sweet soy sauce.
A simple dish that shows off a good chicken. It is gently poached until just cooked, then dipped in ginger and scallion oil.
Cantonese roast goose has crisp, golden skin and juicy meat, and is often served with plum sauce. It is a treat for celebrations.
Rice cooked in a clay pot over fire so the bottom turns crisp, topped with cured sausage or chicken, and finished with a splash of sweet soy sauce.
A silky steamed milk pudding with two thin layers of skin, sweet and smooth, one of the most popular desserts in Guangdong.
A silky congee with fish slices, squid, peanuts and crisp fried strips. It was first sold from small boats on the river.
Cantonese opera combines singing, acrobatics, martial arts and costumes in the Cantonese language. It is a UNESCO intangible heritage and is loved by Cantonese communities worldwide.
Porcelain painted in bright colors and gold in Guangzhou, much of it was made for sale to Europe and is now a collectible art.
Bitter herbal drinks that many in southern China drink to cool the body in the hot, humid weather. Shops sell it by the cup.
A theme park in Shenzhen with miniature versions of the Eiffel Tower, the Pyramids and other famous sights, so you can see the world in one day.
A village in Shenzhen where thousands of painters copy famous artworks and also paint their own creations. It ships paintings all over the world.
The famous electronics market of Shenzhen, where stalls sell chips, phones, drones and every kind of gadget, and where many ideas begin.
Thin slices of fresh beef are dipped in a light broth for a few seconds, then eaten with a sand tea dip. Different cuts have their own names.
Walled villages of the Hakka people, with strong outer walls and houses around a courtyard, built so that clans could defend themselves.
A temple in Foshan dating from the Song dynasty, with beautiful roof ceramics and a hall for martial arts, linked to Wing Chun and Wong Fei-hung.
A memorial hall for Wong Fei-hung, a martial arts master and doctor of Foshan, whose life inspired many kung fu films.
A dragon kiln built on a hillside over 500 years ago that is still fired to make pottery, one of the oldest working kilns in China.
A milk pudding from Shunde, where the dessert is thought to have been born. Shunde is called the food capital of Guangdong.
A festive Junan dish of a whole pig steamed or roasted until the skin is crisp and the meat tender, served at celebrations.
Thin slices of raw freshwater fish eaten with ginger, peanuts, herbs and sauces. It is a Shunde specialty and a shared dish.
Wing Chun is a close-range kung fu style of quick, direct moves, said to have been developed by a woman. Foshan is one of its homes.
Foshan's cut-paper art uses scissors or knives to make flowers, animals and scenes, often in bright colors and for festivals.
A theme park in Zhuhai that rebuilds scenes of the old Yuanmingyuan palace gardens in Beijing, which was burned down in 1860.
Big plump oysters from Hengshan, grilled with garlic and chili and served hot from the grill, a favorite seafood in Zhuhai.
A small, elegant garden in Lingnan style, with a winding layout, halls and a tower with a view over the water.
A museum at the old forts near Humen, where Lin Zexu burned seized opium in 1839, before the start of the First Opium War.
Crisp roast goose from the Qingxi area of Dongguan, with a juicy, flavorful meat and a famous dipping sauce.
Large, savory sticky rice dumplings from Daojiao, filled with pork, beans and egg yolk, made for the Dragon Boat Festival.
Hand-pounded beef balls, so springy that they bounce. A Chaoshan specialty and a proud city dish in Shantou.
A crispy pancake of fresh small oysters in a starchy egg batter, fried until golden and served with fish sauce.
Flat rice noodles, either in a clear broth with meat and herbs or stir-fried over high heat, popular in the Chaoshan area.
Gongfu tea is brewed in tiny cups and a small pot with careful steps. It is the heart of Chaoshan hospitality, and almost every home has a set.
A Buddhist temple in Chaozhou founded in the Tang dynasty and known for its old halls, stone pillars and calm courtyards.
Chaozhou beef balls are known for their bounce and fresh beefy flavor, and are served in a clear soup.
Goose simmered slowly in a spiced master sauce until tender, then sliced and served with garlic vinegar. A famous Chaozhou dish.
Chaozhou carvers cut deep and detailed scenes in wood, covered in gold paint. They decorate temples, halls and old family houses.
Seven limestone peaks that rise from a lake in Zhaoqing, like the stars of the Big Dipper, with caves, bridges and paths.
A nature reserve of ancient forest, streams and waterfalls near Zhaoqing, one of the oldest protected areas in China.
A big pillow-shaped rice dumpling, wrapped in leaves with pork, mung beans and salted egg yolk, steamed for hours.
Duan inkstones are made from a fine stone quarried near Zhaoqing, and are among the most treasured inkstones in China.
A pretty lake in Huizhou with causeways and bridges, where the poet Su Shi lived in exile and wrote about its charm.
A Taoist mountain with temples, waterfalls and herbal gardens, long known in Chinese legends and medicine.
A Hakka dish of chicken wrapped in paper and baked in hot salt, so that the meat is juicy, savory and fragrant.
The village house where Sun Yat-sen was born in 1866, with a small museum about the man who helped end imperial rule.
Grass carp fed with broad beans for weeks until the meat turns firm and crunchy, then cooked and served in Zhongshan.
A young pigeon, roasted until the skin is thin and crispy and the meat juicy, a famous dish of the Shiqi area.
Tall fortified towers, built by families who had worked abroad, that mix Chinese and Western designs. They rise over the fields and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Dried tangerine peel from Xinhui, aged for years like a fine wine, and used in tea, soups and sweets for its warm aroma.
Red sandstone cliffs and peaks that gave the landform Danxia its name. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with fiery colors at sunset.
A famous Chan Buddhist temple about 1,500 years old, associated with the Sixth Patriarch Huineng, a key figure in Chinese Buddhism.
Black tea grown in the hills of northern Guangdong, with a smooth, sweet taste that is the result of a slow drying process.
Squares of tofu stuffed with minced pork and fish, pan-fried and gently simmered, a Hakka comfort food and festive dish.
Chicken baked in hot salt, a Hakka classic with a rich, fragrant, tender result, eaten warm or cold.
A merchant ship of the Song dynasty that sank near the coast, and was lifted whole from the sea, still full of porcelain. It is on show in a museum.
Fermented black soybeans from Yangjiang, salty and deep in flavor, used to season steamed fish, pork and vegetables.
Fresh fish, shrimp and shellfish are on offer at Hailing Island, simply steamed or grilled by the sea.
Fat oysters from the Zhanjiang coast are grilled with garlic and chili or steamed, and are served fresh.
